title: Forms set by physical forces undermine inference of kinship from similarity

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Forms set by physical forces undermine inference of kinship from similarity

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Insofar as forms depend on physical forces and their variations on simple quantitative changes in those forces, similarity of form cannot safely be taken as evidence of consanguinity, and the link between classification and phylogeny must be revised.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But in so far as forms can be shewn to depend on the play of physical forces, and the variations of form to be directly due to simple quantitative variations in these, just so far are we thrown back on our guard before the biological conception of consanguinity, and compelled to revise the vague canons which connect classification with phylogeny.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XII, “The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera”; topic “Physical explanation versus phylogeny”. Scope: Foraminifera and other organisms whose form is governed by physical forces

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch12-14: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.70

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The warning has a clear empirical consequence—physically generated similarity should be homoplastic relative to independent trees. Data can test examples and estimate risk, but cannot settle the normative breadth of how classification 'must' be revised.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For traits with an independently supported physical generative model, quantify homoplasy by mapping form similarity onto molecular phylogenies. Excess similarity among distant relatives under shared physical regimes would show that form alone is unsafe evidence of kinship; close correspondence with independent trees would weaken the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Taxonomic classification uses many characters, not form alone.

The claim is conditional on first demonstrating physical control.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The empirical content is that shell similarity is an unsafe guide to consanguinity wherever form is physically determined. Public sequences and image sets can measure that discordance for planktonic foraminifera and, more thinly, for other groups. The further demand to revise classification is a methodological conclusion that the same discordance does not uniquely dictate. The test is therefore informative about convergence and incomplete as a verdict on taxonomic practice.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Predict genetic or stratigraphic relatedness from shell-shape similarity and compare that prediction with one based on molecular characters. The empirical core is supported if shape neighbors are often distant on sequence trees; it is weakened if shape distance remains a reliable predictor of relatedness after the physically forced characters are removed.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Shape-based names enter both the morphological distances and the labels on many sequences.

How much discordance is enough to 'revise the canons' of classification is a judgment, not a threshold in the claim.
